## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

Liberating structures are frameworks, processes or rules intended to help people and organisations create, innovate and get results without leaving participants constrained or powerless. [AP] The handbook argues that durable change requires changing structural elements, because otherwise change is short-lived. [AR] (p. 6, "Introduction")

> For things to really change, structural elements need to change, too. Otherwise change is short-lived.
>
> [V] (p. 6, "Introduction")

The interaction designs the handbook favours are deliberately messy and complex: their conversations cross departmental, role and organisational boundaries; many self-organise through local interaction; and their dialogue is generative. [AP] Their effectiveness depends on combining that freedom with just enough structure to channel energy and keep work productive. [AR] (p. 6, "Introduction")

Jazz supplies the handbook's governing analogy. Underlying principles let people who have not met play together while preserving both a recognisable piece and room for unique expression. [AE] The argument is that a small collection of principles can simultaneously preserve identity and create extensive freedom. [AR] (p. 6, "Introduction")

> The guidelines of jazz are a collection of principles that give enough structure so that people can create together. These same principles make possible infinite degrees of freedom.
>
> [V] (p. 6, "Introduction")

The handbook ties that structural thesis to ownership. Ownership exists when people participate in developing an idea, decision, action plan or choice and freely make it their own; buy-in begins after somebody else has already thought and decided, leaving others to be convinced to implement. [AP] The source argues that aiming for buy-in produces weak implementation and mediocre results, while people confronting intractable socio-technical behavioural problems need to own new behaviours. [AR] (p. 7, "Ownership versus Buy-In")

The closing pattern-language account generalises the catalogue. Liberating structures vary the rhythm and timing of interaction, boundaries of group size and inclusion, physical containers such as space and room set-up, and conceptual containers created by the wording of a question. [AP] Those components can be combined in dozens of ways, putting high-engagement design within everyday reach rather than reserving it for multi-day consultant-led events. [AR] (pp. 59–60, "Origins"; "A Pattern Language for Engagement")

## Part I: Conditions for engagement

### Ownership rather than buy-in

Ownership means participating in development and freely choosing; buy-in means being asked to adopt what others developed and decided. [AP] The handbook treats talk of buy-in as evidence that the development and implementation process may have omitted people who should have been involved. [AR] (p. 7, "Ownership versus Buy-In")

> Anytime you or someone around you thinks or talks about buy-in, beware!
>
> [V] (p. 7, "Ownership versus Buy-In")

The source's positive formulation is equally direct: “Liberating Structures are all about creating ownership.” [V] (p. 7, "Ownership versus Buy-In")

### Space, proximity and aesthetics

Many meetings work well without tables because chairs can move among configurations. [AP] Where writing or drawing requires tables, the handbook favours small café tables seating four to six; it says typical large round conference tables put people too far apart for lively conversation. [AP] Elbow room and access to open space also matter because some exercises work best while participants stand. [AP] (p. 8, "Choosing Space")

Natural light is preferred to artificial, especially fluorescent, light. [AP] Colour, flowers and natural materials can make the room more welcoming, while a long paper-covered wall—or poster board on easels—can support graphic recording by a professional or by participants. [AP] (p. 9, "Aesthetics Are Important")

The methods remain usable in constrained spaces. [AP] In fixed seating, participants can stand, turn to a row behind them, or form groups of three in aisles or spare areas; around round tables they can move away from the furniture; with movable rows, chairs can at least be turned to face one another. [AE] (p. 10, "Working with the Space You’re Given")

### Storyboard design

A storyboard can replace an agenda for a meeting, event or longer initiative. [AP] It can carry ordinary planning information—roles, topics, questions, timings and materials—while also representing what participants will experience. [AP] Because the proposed flow is visible, a group can design collaboratively and notice, for example, a disengaging run of podium sessions. [AE] Movable post-it notes can represent components so alternative sequences can be tried. [AP] (p. 11, "Storyboard Design and Planning")

### Nothing about people without them

Searching for unusually effective behaviour and solutions requires widening conversations to include the people most involved, especially people who do not normally speak with one another. [AR] The handbook illustrates this with a nurse who connects glove use to inadequate supplies, prompting contact with somebody in supplies, and with a proposed change to doctors' rounding behaviour, prompting consultation with doctors themselves. [AE] (p. 12, "Nothing About Me Without Me")

“Who’s not here that could contribute to our conversation?” is the key question for engaging unusual suspects. [V] The source advises widening the network and adding more voices, while recognising that people previously invited as window dressing may distrust invitations that promise participation. [AP] (p. 13, "Engage the Unusual Suspects")

## Part II: Liberating Structures catalogue

### Opening, reflection and individual voice

#### Knee-to-Knee Conversation

The source attributes the power of small groups sitting knee-to-knee without a table to Peter Block and points readers to `asmallgroup.net`. [BT] It recommends arranging small chair groups before arrival, encouraging people to sit with less-familiar participants, and opening with a purpose-related question such as what drew them to the meeting or what audacious goal the group could have. [AP] (p. 14, "Knee-to-Knee Conversation")

#### One Minute of Silence

A full minute of silence before an exercise gives every participant—not only introverts—time to reflect, arrive mentally and leave the previous meeting, call or journey behind. [AP] The facilitator can announce that the minute will be timed exactly and later ask what the silence contributed. [AE] (p. 15, "One Minute of Silence")

#### Take 10 (Minutes)

An individually held interval—seven, ten, fifteen or another suitable number of minutes—can deepen a conversation, including in a short meeting. [AP] Participants may make private notes in response to a demanding question, then share through a small-group structure. [AP] (p. 18, "Take 10 (Minutes)")

#### Take a Panel

Each participant receives a wall-mounted sheet and responds independently to eight to ten generative questions using words, drawings, diagrams or mind maps. [AP] After about 20 minutes, participants meet the two or three people around them and give each person about four minutes to bring their stand-alone panel to life, sharing only what makes a difference and taking clarification questions. [AP] The method can serve as a soft start if every arrival still gets enough time. [AP] (p. 19, "Take a Panel")

#### Six Words

The source says Hemingway was once challenged to write a six-word novel and gives “For sale: baby shoes, never worn.” [BT] It says Larry Smith turned that idea into the Six-Word Memoir and that the Mulago Foundation applies a related discipline to mission statements: fewer than eight words, a verb, a target population and a measurable outcome. [BT] The handbook uses constrained word counts to get beneath vague mission, vision, purpose and strategy language. [AP] (p. 23, "Six Words")

#### 5 Whys

The 5 Whys is presented as a question-asking technique for exploring cause-and-effect relationships and root causes, extended here to questions of purpose. [AP] One partner listens actively, poses a question and asks “WHY?” at least five times, with variants such as why the answer matters; partners then reverse roles. [AP] The source explicitly permits continuing beyond five until enough layers have been removed to reach what participants regard as a fundamental truth. [AP] (p. 25, "5 Whys")

#### Impromptu Speed Networking

Participants leave their belongings, stand in open space, reflect on a provocative question with no right answer, and repeatedly pair with people they know less well. [AP] A bell closes each five-to-ten-minute conversation; three rounds are described as usually sufficient. [AP] The design gives everybody an early first contribution, and the source claims that in a 30-minute session every participant can receive 12–15 minutes of airtime regardless of total attendance. [AP] (p. 26, "Impromptu Speed Networking")

#### 1-2-4-Whole Group

The sequence moves from a couple of minutes of silent individual reflection to pairs, then to groups of four to six, then to an open whole-group question. [AP] The source cautions that more than six people in the small-group phase is too large to give everybody a chance to speak. [AP] It can stand alone or combine with Impromptu Speed Networking. [AP] (p. 27, "1-2-4-Whole Group")

### Interviews, questions and distributed expertise

#### Celebrity Interviews

A conversational “talk show” can replace a traditional presentation or panel when one or more people carry information or ideas that may catalyse the room. [AP] The source lists five intended effects: convey a small number of memorable ideas; create appetite for deeper material; show a key player's relationship, personality and passion; establish an interactive tone; and avoid the energy loss associated with listening to one voice for more than five minutes, especially when it delivers text-heavy data. [AP] Questions should open rather than narrow the exchange; asking what surprised somebody in marketing data is offered as an alternative to asking merely what the data say. [AE] (p. 16, "Celebrity Interviews")

#### Taking Questions

Questions or comments are taken in batches of three or four rather than one by one. [AP] This reduces the chance that the first question pulls the exchange in an odd direction, interrupts the repeated question-answer pattern, and surfaces more of the group's distributed intelligence. [AR] Questions can be captured on post-its or cards, after which the interviewer or facilitator can invite the featured speakers to combine or select among them. [AP] (p. 17, "Taking Questions")

#### A Note About “Report Outs”

> “Report Outs” from breakout sessions are **BORING!!!**
>
> [V] (p. 20, "A Note About “Report Outs”")

The handbook argues that serial summaries usually drain the life from small-group conversations. [AR] It favours carrying the experience into a new conversation, where important material can return as part of a fresh integration. [AP] If documentation is genuinely needed, participants should help determine who needs it and the most useful form. [AP] (p. 20, "A Note About “Report Outs”")

#### Wise Crowds

Groups of five or six sit knee-to-knee, with one client and the others acting as a consulting team. [AP] The source specifies three phases: the client sketches a complex challenge for about ten minutes with only limited clarification; the client turns away and listens without responding while the team talks independently for at least 15 minutes; then the client turns back, identifies what intrigued, surprised or resonated, and rejoins a free conversation. [AP] The consulting team offers questions, paraphrases, metaphors, examples and musings rather than deciding what the client ought to do. [AP] (p. 21, "Wise Crowds")

#### Appreciative Interviews

The source argues that what people focus on tends to grow, so attention to what works creates a context for more progress. [AR] Partners alternate between telling a positive “time when” story and interviewing with curiosity, empathy, generative questions and tolerance for ambiguity and silence. [AP] The interviewer listens for stories and quotations without substituting their own experience or opinion. [AP] The source identifies Appreciative Interviews as part of Appreciative Inquiry and points to `appreciativeinquiry.case.edu`. [BT] (p. 28, "Appreciative Interviews")

#### Discovery & Action Dialogues

Discovery & Action Dialogues have three stated purposes: discover existing and new solutions to a target problem through short, lively conversations; identify volunteers to experiment; and let facilitators and participants hear barriers to action or change. [AP] Seven prompts move from what participants know and do, through barriers and exceptions, to ideas, next conditions and “who will do what when next”. [AP] The source says the process was developed through Plexus Institute's Positive Deviance work and applied by the handbook's authors to hospital quality and safety problems. [BT] (p. 29, "Discovery & Action Dialogues")

#### Q Storming

Participants generate one legibly written question per post-it, including courageous, provocative, silly and “dumb” questions related to the meeting's purpose. [AP] The questions can then be grouped, categorised, prioritised, read aloud, discussed for patterns or used to launch Just in Time Topics. [AP] The source quotes Diana Whitney, identified as an originator of Appreciative Inquiry, saying “Questions are fateful ! ” and says Marilee G. Adams originally developed Q-Storming. [BT] (p. 44, "Q Storming")

### Self-organisation, scenarios and strategic sense-making

#### Participatory Scenarios

The handbook contrasts expert- or small-team-created scenarios with whole-community scenario development, arguing that community ownership makes scenarios more likely to enter decision-making. [AR] Its five-step sequence is: identify five or six dimensions of relevant drivers; put any two dimensions on a matrix; fill the resulting landscape with characteristics, consequences, questions or opportunities and challenges; create and name a vivid scenario story; and repeat with other combinations. [AP] “Virtually Vanilla” is the source's sample scenario name. [AE] (p. 22, "Participatory Scenarios")

#### Just in Time Topics

Participants silently write a question, story or problem they want to discuss, usually for 45–90 minutes, then briefly declare and post it. [AP] Locations are assigned, after which people choose where to spend their time; the source discourages combining topics merely because they are related, since smaller discussions are more satisfying. [AP] Two offered laws are “Whoever comes are the right people.” [V] and “The law of two feet.” [V] Under the second, a participant who is neither contributing nor receiving value moves elsewhere. [AP] The process is identified as inspired by Open Space. [BT] (p. 24, "Just in Time Topics")

#### TRIZ

The handbook describes TRIZ as a problem-solving, analysis and forecasting tool derived from patterns of invention, developed by Soviet inventor and science-fiction author Genrich Altshuller and colleagues in the 1940s, and commonly translated as the Theory of Inventive Problem Solving. [BT] It uses one part of that wider approach: specify the desired result; design a system certain to prevent it; find similarities with the current state; and identify how to eliminate those similarities. [AP] The source points readers to `triz.co.uk` and says TRIZ emerged from engineering. [BT] (p. 30, "TRIZ")

#### Wicked Questions

Wicked questions expose assumptions and differences so a group can seek common ground or creative alternatives. [AP] A wicked question contains a paradox or tension but has no obvious answer; unlike a trick question, nobody already knows the answer. [AP] The source contrasts questions that hold both quality standards and local innovation, or top-down safety discipline and bottom-up creativity, with a blame-framed complaint about headquarters. [AE] (p. 31, "Wicked Questions")

#### 15% Solutions

The source presents a claim attributed to Gareth Morgan in *The Globe and Mail*: people have about 15 per cent control over their work, while broader structures, systems, events and culture shape the other 85 per cent. [BT] It argues for mobilising small 15-per-cent initiatives that can accumulate into transformational change, guided by shared vision and self-organisation. [BT] The handbook asks where participants are free to act and says this conversation works well with Troika. [AP] (p. 32, "15% Solutions")

#### Agreement/Uncertainty Matrix

The source attributes to Ralph Stacey a matrix distinguishing situations by the degree of certainty about what is happening and the degree of agreement about meaning or action. [BT] It attributes to Brenda Zimmerman the comparison of a recipe as simple, an aeroplane as complicated and raising a child as complex. [BT] The handbook argues that strategies for simple and complicated situations often fail in complex ones because the latter are emergent and unpredictable, and invites participants to map their work on the matrix. [AR] (p. 36, "Agreement/Uncertainty Matrix")

#### 25-to-10

Each person writes an unsigned idea on a card. [AP] Participants repeatedly mill, exchange cards, read the card they receive persuasively, and rate it from one to five. [AP] The source specifies five rounds, producing five ratings per card and a maximum score of 25; the facilitator counts down from 25 and has the holders read high-scoring cards until the top ten or another required number is identified. [AP] All cards are retained because initially unremarkable ideas may become useful later. [AP] The source explicitly says the method is not recommended for making a decision; it is for sensing the crowd's wisdom. [AP] (p. 37, "25-to-10")

#### Simple Rules

The handbook says patterns arise from simple rules: constraints that create room for creativity while retaining critical elements. [AP] It names five possible rule types—How To, Boundary, Priority, Timing and Exit—and gives four steps: select an activity that could be reinvented; imagine handing it to a design team; specify the few mandatory elements; then test every proposed rule by asking what happens if it is removed. [AP] The debrief examines over- and under-specification. [AP] (p. 45, "Simple Rules")

#### Portfolio Planning

The source says groups benefit from seeing the whole rather than discussing one part at a time. [AP] It attributes to Brenda Zimmerman an eco-cycle account using forest-fire phases, including the importance of creative destruction for renewal. [BT] Participants place activities within a portfolio across the eco-cycle, either in small groups or on a wall-sized version with movable post-its; the source points to The Grove for discussion templates. [AP] (p. 47, "Portfolio Planning")

### Structured dialogue and circulating groups

#### Conversation Café Dialogue

The source lists six agreements: open-mindedness, acceptance, curiosity, discovery, sincerity and brevity. [AP] Groups of six to eight use a talking object through four stages: a first brief round with no response; a second round that deepens each person's comments; open dialogue; and a final brief statement of what challenged, touched or inspired each participant. [AP] The holder speaks while others listen, preventing ordinary back-and-forth during the rounds. [AP] (p. 33, "Conversation Café Dialogue")

#### World Café

World Café is presented as a way for a very large group to experience one whole conversation. [AP] A café-like setting uses small tables with four chairs, paper, coloured pens, flowers and an optional talking object. [AP] The host welcomes participants and explains the process; three or more 20-minute small-group rounds move participants among tables, optionally leaving a host to brief the next group. [AP] Context-specific questions frame each round, and a harvest makes insights visible to the large group. [AP] The source points to `theworldcafe.com` for further resources. [BT] (p. 34, "World Café")

#### Troika Consulting

Three people sit knee-to-knee, with one acting as timekeeper so each receives equal time. [AP] After individual reflection on a difficult question, each ten-minute round lets one participant describe a challenge, receive clarifying questions, and then hear partners explore possibilities with one another and with the participant. [AP] Roles rotate through all three people before a closing conversation about cross-round patterns. [AP] (p. 35, "Troika Consulting")

#### After Action Debrief: What, So What, Now What?

The source specifies three questions in order: **What?** asks what is emerging, what data stand out and what happened; **So What?** asks what the data imply and what patterns matter; **Now What?** asks what action may help and who else should be involved. [AP] It says the exercise is included in many Center for Creative Leadership creative-thinking and leadership programmes. [BT] (p. 38, "After Action Debrief: What, So What, Now What?")

#### Gallery Walk

Gallery Walk is offered as an alternative to report-outs. [AP] Teams put what they want to share on posters; one member stays nearby to answer questions while others walk the gallery, with team members able to rotate that duty. [AP] A following small-group conversation can ask what participants noticed, what themes or surprises appeared, what was new and how the material changes the conversation. [AP] (p. 39, "Gallery Walk")

#### Fishbowl

A centre circle of five or six chairs sits inside a larger circle. [AP] People with direct experience discuss the challenge with one another rather than addressing the audience; the outer group then asks questions and offers insights while the centre listens; finally the two circles enter dialogue. [AP] The suggested debrief asks what surprised listeners, how their perspective changed and which questions remain open. [AP] (p. 42, "Fishbowl")

#### Shift & Share

Shift & Share circulates participants among teams with experience stories, research or plans, avoiding linear didactic reporting. [AP] The source's six numbered design points cover recruiting volunteer teams, choosing their number to fit attendance and time, coaching executive-briefing-level show-and-tell material, assigning locations, rotating participants, and selecting one or more rounds. [AP] Its worked timing examples compare five teams in one hour using 15-minute visits with choosing three of five teams for 20 minutes each. [AE] (p. 46, "Shift & Share")

### Embodied mapping, networks and action

#### Mini Constellations

An object represents an idea or choice. [AP] Participants place themselves nearer or farther according to how positively they feel, then speak from the perspective of that distance, beginning with the farthest ring. [AP] A later round can map expected success or likelihood, opening discussion of the difference between feeling and assessment. [AP] The source says Constellations is rooted in family therapy and describes this exercise as a very small part of a broader body of work. [BT] (p. 40, "Mini Constellations")

#### Levels of Accountability

The page presents eight labelled stances: Denial, Blame others, Blame self, Wait ’n Hope, Acknowledge situation, Accept ownership, Find Solutions, and Take Action and Learn. [AP] It associates these with phrases ranging from “This has nothing to do with me” and “It’s their fault” to “It starts with me”, “This can work”, and “Make it happen, renewal”, then asks what is needed to work “above the line”. [AP] (p. 41, "Levels of Accountability")

#### Network Weaving

Participants map people and organisations important to a project, goal or initiative, then share the map with two or three others. [AP] Questions identify surprises, missing participants, hubs, isolates and underrepresented perspectives. [AP] Follow-on moves close triangles by introducing useful unconnected pairs, integrate clusters around shared projects, and expand the periphery to add resources, ideas, skills and perspectives. [AP] (p. 43, "Network Weaving")

#### Improv Games

The source offers improv games as practice in opening rather than closing conversations and building on others' ideas. [AP] It describes three games: a group tells a story one word at a time; pairs begin every contribution with “YES AND” and thereby reveal attempts to control or reject the offer; and participants improvise movements with coffee filters, imitate partners and notice what occurs. [AP] The source credits the coffee-filter activity to Tom Sparough, “The Space Painter”. [BT] (pp. 48, "Improv Games")

## Part III: Seeing complexity and complex systems

The handbook explicitly says the three following activities are not themselves Liberating Structures; they catalyse conversations about complex systems. [AP] (p. 49, "Seeing Complexity and Complex Systems")

### Complex Systems Game: How Many Ways?

The exercise is intended to let participants discover that complex systems are socially constructed rather than objective truth. [AP] Groups receive bags containing 12–25 similar but non-identical random objects, organise them by a chosen criterion without labels, and may try multiple arrangements before choosing an “elegant”, easy-to-guess, hard-to-guess or meta-level structure. [AP] Groups inspect and guess one another's criteria, then discuss whether right answers exist, what shaped their organisation, which assumptions mattered, how they negotiated and what surprised them. [AP] (p. 50, "Complex Systems Game: How Many Ways?")

### Tic Tac Toe

Pairs face one another under two rules—no talking and no touching—and play several three-by-three games in the air before attempting four-by-four. [AP] The source says most people can manage three-by-three after some practice but find four-by-four impossible. [AP] It uses the contrast to argue that meetings often assume shared subjects, definitions and assumptions without taking enough time to build the common understanding needed for complex work. [AR] (p. 51, "Tic Tac Toe")

### A Place in the System

Standing participants privately choose a Person A and Person B, then try first to get between them and later to stay equidistant from them. [AP] The group moves and eventually approaches a relatively stable configuration before reflecting on each round. [AP] The exercise opens discussion of planning when important factors are outside individual control and everything is moving. [AP] (p. 52, "A Place in the System")

## Part IV: Small conditions that help the structures thrive

The source labels these five pages “random thoughts” about conditions in which Liberating Structures can thrive. [AP] (p. 53, "Random Thoughts")

### Waving Hands versus Clapping

Some groups acknowledge a contribution by waving hands rather than clapping; the handbook says this can register appreciation without breaking the mood. [AP] (p. 54, "Waving Hands versus Clapping")

### Talking Objects

The handbook offers a “talking object” as a potentially more comfortable alternative where talking-stick traditions carry a spiritual aspect, and says the object can be anything, including a pen or rubber duck. [AP] It quotes Dr. Locust of the American Research and Training Center in Tucson describing talking sticks in Native American council circles as a means of just and impartial hearing, passed until all who wanted to speak had done so, and explaining symbolic associations of an eagle feather and rabbit fur. [BT] (p. 55, "Talking Objects")

### Music & Poetry

Music on arrival and participant-offered music or poetry are suggested as conditions for creativity and unconventional thought. [AP] The source notes that more participants may volunteer than expected. [AP] (p. 56, "Music & Poetry")

### Tingsha Bells

Because the structures often move participants among groups and spaces, the facilitator needs a way to call them back. [AP] The source rejects yelling and microphone tapping as abrasive or grating, recommends portable Tingsha bells whose sound carries, and notes that children's xylophones also work. [AP] (p. 57, "Tingsha Bells")

### Take 20 Seconds

When real conversation matters more than supplying all the “right” answers, the facilitator asks a good question and waits at least 20 seconds. [AP] The source says facilitators begin speaking after six seconds on average; speaking that soon can interrupt people forming answers and gathering courage, while implying that the facilitator holds the answers. [AP] Looking at one's shoes can break eye contact, signal reflection and reduce pressure to speak. [AE] (p. 58, "Take 20 Seconds")

## Part V: Origins and a pattern language for engagement

### Origins named by the source

The source says William Torbert first introduced the idea of liberating structures in *The Power of Balance: Transforming Self, Society, and Scientific Inquiry* (1991). [BT] It connects his interest in integral leadership and action inquiry to organisational forms that guide people while developing their ability to guide themselves, and to theories of generative power and continual quality improvement. [BT] (p. 59, "Origins")

Edward de Bono's *Teaching Thinking* (1991) is quoted distinguishing restricting from liberating structures and describing tools as liberating structures through which students can surprise themselves with new ideas. [BT] (p. 59, "Origins")

The handbook says the connection to process design emerged as facilitators and organisational-development specialists developed large-group methods over the preceding 20 years. [AP] It attributes to Dick Axelrod's *Terms of Engagement* (2nd ed., 2010) principles across Open Space, Appreciative Inquiry, the Conference Model and other large-group methods: widen involvement, connect people and ideas, create communities for action, and practise democratic principles. [BT] (p. 59, "Origins")

The source notes that Open Space Technology combines four principles, one law and common practices to support self-organisation around any topic. [AP] It contrasts such comprehensive strategies—which often span days or separated sessions and use consultant teams—with the need to sustain engagement in everyday meetings. [AR] (pp. 59–60, "Origins"; "A Pattern Language for Engagement")

### Pattern language

Powerful large-group events can produce ideas and impact, but their energy and commitment may decay when people return to default meeting practices. [AR] The source therefore asks how to extend that half-life, make enlivening engagement available every day, and put the capacity to host it into everybody's hands. [AP] (p. 60, "A Pattern Language for Engagement")

The handbook attributes the idea of a pattern language to Christopher Alexander's *A Pattern Language* (1977), developed for architecture and community environments. [BT] Alexander's “intimacy gradient” is the worked example: bedroom, study, common area or kitchen, and entrance or porch offer recognisable degrees of intimacy whose vocabulary helps designers, planners, architects and community members discuss choices. [BT] (p. 60, "A Pattern Language for Engagement")

Peter and Trudy Johnson-Lenz are credited with treating rhythms, boundaries and containers as fundamental patterns of social life. [BT] Rhythms shape recurring contact; boundaries shape connection and separation; physical and social containers frame meetings; and skilful use of these elements is described as a critical facilitator capacity. [BT] (p. 60, "A Pattern Language for Engagement")

Applied to engagement, the source says liberating structures offer choices in four component families: interaction rhythm and timing, boundaries of group size and inclusion, physical containers, and conceptual containers created by question wording. [AP] These simple components can be recombined in dozens of ways. [AP] (p. 60, "A Pattern Language for Engagement")

> All liberating structures are made up of these simple sets of components that can be combined in dozens of different ways.
>
> [V] (p. 60, "A Pattern Language for Engagement")

## Positions the source explicitly frames against

- **Buy-in as a substitute for participation and ownership.** The source calls buy-in the opposite of ownership and treats the term as a danger signal that essential involvement is missing. [AR] (p. 7, "Ownership versus Buy-In")
- **Room arrangements that hold people apart.** Large round tables are described as too large for lively conversation, and even constrained rooms should be adapted to bring people closer. [AP] (pp. 8–10, "Choosing Space"; "Working with the Space You’re Given")
- **Long sequences of podium sessions.** The storyboard example treats a row of podium sessions as visibly disengaging. [AE] (p. 11, "Storyboard Design and Planning")
- **Inviting people as window dressing.** The source notes that prior invitations without real contribution create justified suspicion. [AP] (p. 13, "Engage the Unusual Suspects")
- **One voice dominating for more than five minutes.** Celebrity Interviews are designed in part to avoid the energy loss associated with lengthy single-voice delivery, especially of text-heavy data. [AP] (p. 16, "Celebrity Interviews")
- **Serial question-answer patterns and report-outs.** Batched questions distribute intelligence, while serial breakout summaries are rejected as boring and draining. [AR] (pp. 17, 20, "Taking Questions"; "A Note About “Report Outs”")
- **Expert-owned scenarios.** The source says scenarios made by experts or small teams may lack community ownership and therefore fail to influence decisions. [AR] (p. 22, "Participatory Scenarios")
- **Combining every related discussion topic.** Just in Time Topics favours smaller self-selected discussions rather than collapsing related proposals together. [AP] (p. 24, "Just in Time Topics")
- **Treating wicked questions as tricks or blame statements.** Wicked questions hold a real paradox with no known answer; a complaint that headquarters staff are “bozos” is given as a non-example. [AP] [AE] (p. 31, "Wicked Questions")
- **Using crowd ratings as a decision.** The source explicitly limits 25-to-10 to sensing ideas and says it is not recommended for decision-making. [AP] (p. 37, "25-to-10")
- **Linear, didactic reporting.** Gallery Walk and Shift & Share circulate participants and conversation instead. [AP] (pp. 39, 46, named headings)
- **Over- or under-specifying constraints.** Simple Rules tests whether each proposed constraint is truly mandatory. [AP] (p. 45, "Simple Rules")
- **Assuming common understanding in complex work.** The four-by-four Tic Tac Toe exercise argues that shared words do not guarantee shared definitions and assumptions. [AR] (p. 51, "Tic Tac Toe")
- **Yelling or tapping a microphone to recall groups.** The source calls these abrasive or grating and offers bells or a xylophone. [AP] (p. 57, "Tingsha Bells")
- **A facilitator answering their own question too soon.** Speaking before participants have formed answers can truncate reflection and imply that the facilitator owns the answers. [AR] (p. 58, "Take 20 Seconds")
- **Engagement confined to occasional large events.** The pattern-language argument seeks everyday access to high-engagement structures because event energy often fades on return to default meetings. [AR] (pp. 59–60, "Origins"; "A Pattern Language for Engagement")

## Citation and source-integrity notes

The supplied source is a 2,767-line Markdown transcription of a 60-page handbook. It preserves the cover attribution, 2010 date, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 licence statement, table of contents, printed page-boundary numerals from 2 through 60, and named headings for every substantive page. The citation style therefore uses printed page number plus heading.

The complete line range was read. Every item in the source's table of contents appears in the anchor list and body above. The 35-entry catalogue count was verified against both the table of contents and the uninterrupted one-entry-per-page run from pages 14 through 48. The three complex-systems exercises and five random-thought notes were likewise verified against their framing pages and headings.

The supplied Markdown flattens some visual layout. Most notably, the Agreement/Uncertainty Matrix's diagram is not represented as an image, and the Levels of Accountability page is a sequence of labels and phrases whose spatial relationships are only partly recoverable. This reference reports the preserved prose and labels but does not reconstruct missing geometry. The Just in Time Topics page survives as a two-column Markdown table and was read in full.

No information from another reference or corpus was introduced. Named-person and named-organisation attributions appear only where this source itself names them, and they are marked `[BT]`. No cross-corpus Connections section is included.
